items.caption:
Sam Altman says people spend too much time preparing to do the thing instead of just doing it.

Asked how he learned to run Y Combinator and OpenAI, he says for jobs few people have done, you learn as you go. You will make a lot of mistakes, but if you run experiments and reflect on them (deliberate practice, not random flailing), you get good surprisingly fast.

What is one thing you have been preparing for instead of starting?

Source: Stanford GSB, View From The Top with Sam Altman (co-founder and CEO of OpenAI). Full video: youtube.com/watch?v=anAmTGcewX8

In 2015, Ali Ghodsi heard through the grapevine that the Databricks board was interviewing other people for the CEO job.

Apache Spark was a hit, but GAAP revenue that year was only about $1.5M. He never wanted to be CEO, applied for a faculty job at Berkeley and was planning to take it.

Would you have stayed or gone back to your dream job?

items.caption:
Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi says the number one trait that is terrible for a CEO is being conflict-averse.

He is clear that conflict-averse people are often wonderful people. But everyone is pushing a CEO for something, and if you avoid conflict you end up saying yes, lying, or dodging the subject.

Agree or disagree: can a conflict-averse person be a great CEO?

items.caption:
Mark Cuban asked ChatGPT to design a competitor to a food company's number one cookie, sitting with the company's boss.

He asked for a cheaper, more GLP-1 friendly version with a full bill of materials, sources and manufacturing steps. In about three minutes they had it back, and the executive had no idea.

Which big brand do you think is most exposed to this?

Source: a16z, Mark Cuban on Why AI Could Turn Solo Founders Into Trillionaires. Full video: youtube.com/watch?v=5UWDUD6qaM4
